title: Arm to Arm: The Vaccine Goes Round the World
subtitle: Jenner's cowpox and the Royal Philanthropic Vaccine Expedition — Berkeley, Boston, Monticello, Bombay, the Spanish Indies, Manila, Macao and Canton, 1796–1806
intro: On 14 May 1796 Edward Jenner, a country surgeon in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, took matter from a cowpox sore on the hand of the dairymaid Sarah Nelmes and put it into two small cuts on the arm of James Phipps, an eight-year-old boy from a local labouring family. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with smallpox matter, and nothing happened. Jenner had tested his idea on a child who could not consent; the book he printed in 1798, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, numbered Phipps as Case XVII among other children used the same way.

The new 'vaccine' (from vacca, cow) had one great weakness: it did not keep. Dried on threads, glass or lancets it often died in transit, and over a long sea voyage it almost always did. The only reliable way to carry it was in a living body, passing it from the ripe pustule of one unvaccinated person to the next every nine or ten days. That is how it crossed oceans in this chapter: arm to arm.

The Spanish crown's answer was the Royal Philanthropic Vaccine Expedition. Under a Royal Order of 1 September 1803 the military physician Francisco Javier de Balmis sailed from A Coruña on the corvette María Pita on 30 November 1803 with twenty-two boys aged about three to nine — foundlings from the orphanages of A Coruña and Santiago, plus Benito Vélez, the adopted son of the orphanage rectoress Isabel Zendal (spelled Sendales, Zendala and Gómez Sandalla in Balmis's own papers). The boys were the vaccine's container. Two at a time were vaccinated from the previous pair. They had no say. Later legs used more children: 26 Mexican boys across the Pacific to Manila, three Filipino boys to Macao, and children taken from Venezuela, Cartagena and Cuba, including enslaved children.

The expedition did not arrive in a vacuum. In Puerto Rico the surgeon Francisco Oller had been vaccinating for weeks with lymph from the Danish island of St Thomas; in Havana Tomás Romay had already begun; in Mexico the viceroy disputed Balmis's numbers; in Macao a Portuguese trader's crew had brought the vaccine from Manila before Balmis did, and the East India Company surgeon Alexander Pearson and his Chinese pupil Qiu Xi were spreading it in Canton. By other roads it had reached Boston (Benjamin Waterhouse, 1800), Thomas Jefferson's Monticello (1801) and Bombay (1802), where a three-year-old girl, Anna Dusthall, became the source of much of India's vaccine.

The record is mostly letters, official reports, lists and treatises rather than diaries, and it is uneven. Physicians and officials wrote; the children who carried the vaccine, and Isabel Zendal who nursed them, left no surviving firsthand accounts — they appear only in other people's lists and letters, and this chapter says so wherever they appear. Disputes about priority (who vaccinated first, whose lymph was genuine) and about whether cowpox protected at all are given as the positions people held at the time.
A coda points east: Japan obtained viable vaccine only in 1849, when scabs sent from Batavia to the Dutch post at Dejima took in children vaccinated in Nagasaki — half a century after Phipps.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Spain, Britain, the United States and their colonies used the Gregorian calendar throughout. Chinese sources (Qiu Xi's treatise) used the lunisolar calendar with reign years; only Western years are given here, at year or month precision. Some itinerary dates differ by a day or more between modern accounts (for example the Acapulco sailing, 8 or 9 February 1805, and Balmis's audience with Charles IV, given as 7 or 17 September 1806); the date used is stated and the alternative noted.

eyes.name: Edward Jenner
eyes.role: Country physician and surgeon in Berkeley, Gloucestershire; Fellow of the Royal Society; aged 46 in 1796
eyes.form: published case reports and dated letters
eyes.authenticity: The Inquiry (London: Sampson Low, 1798) and its sequels (1799, 1800, and The Origin of the Vaccine Inoculation, 1801) are Jenner's own printed texts. Many letters were printed by John Baron in The Life of Edward Jenner (1827–38); some survive in manuscript at the Wellcome Collection and Royal College of Physicians.
eyes.bio: Jenner set out to prove a piece of dairy-country lore: that milkmaids who had caught cowpox did not take smallpox. His proof rested on deliberately exposing vaccinated children to smallpox. He then spent the rest of his life as the vaccine's advocate, distributing lymph and instructions worldwide, including to the Spanish expedition's route.

sources.title: James Lind Library: Jenner 1798 Inquiry (cases and summary)
King's College London: Jenner on smallpox (1798 plates)

eyes.name: Benjamin Waterhouse
eyes.role: Professor of the theory and practice of physic at Harvard; aged 46 in 1800
eyes.vantage_label: the first vaccinator in the United States
eyes.authenticity: A Prospect of Exterminating the Small-Pox (Cambridge, Mass., 1800; Part II 1802) is his own text. His letters to Jefferson survive in the Jefferson Papers and are edited in Founders Online.
eyes.bio: Waterhouse had studied medicine in Britain and read Jenner's Inquiry. In summer 1800 he obtained cowpox matter from England and tried it first on his own children and household. Wanting national backing, he sent his pamphlet and then live matter to the Vice-President, Thomas Jefferson.

sources.title: Monticello: Benjamin Waterhouse
Indiana University Libraries: The Many Roads to Vaccination (US)

eyes.name: Thomas Jefferson
eyes.role: Vice-President, then (from March 1801) third President of the United States; planter and enslaver at Monticello
eyes.vantage_label: the planter who vaccinated his household
eyes.authenticity: Letters edited in The Papers of Thomas Jefferson and published on Founders Online (National Archives); recipient copies at the Massachusetts Historical Society, press copies at the Library of Congress.
eyes.bio: Jefferson ran his own vaccination trial at Monticello in August 1801, counting which arms 'took'. The people he called his family or household included the enslaved people of Monticello, who were vaccinated alongside his relatives and neighbours; they had no say. His letters are a running case ledger.

sources.title: Founders Online: TJ to Waterhouse, 25 Dec 1800
Founders Online: TJ to Waterhouse, 8 Aug 1801
Founders Online: TJ to Waterhouse, 21 Aug 1801
TJ to Jenner, 14 May 1806 (text)

eyes.name: Anna Dusthall
eyes.role: A three-year-old girl in Bombay, described in later accounts as of mixed parentage
eyes.vantage_label: the child whose arm carried India's vaccine
eyes.form: named in East India Company medical records (no surviving firsthand account found)
eyes.authenticity: No surviving firsthand account found. She is known from the Bombay surgeons' reports of 1802–03 as retold in modern histories; those histories credit the Bombay medical service (Helenus Scott is named for the first successful Bombay vaccination of 1802). The day, 14 June 1802, is the date usually given and has not been checked against the original report here.
eyes.bio: Lymph sent overland from Europe via Baghdad and Basra was tried on about twenty Bombay children; only Anna's arm produced a usable pustule. Matter from it went to five more children and into vials sent inland, and modern accounts say Indian vaccine for years descended from that single arm.

sources.title: ThePrint excerpt: S. S. Yadav, India's Vaccine Growth Story
Homegrown: The journey of India's first vaccine
Helenus Scott (biography)

eyes.name: Francisco Javier de Balmis y Berenguer
eyes.role: Military surgeon and physician to Charles IV; director of the Royal Philanthropic Vaccine Expedition; aged 50 at sailing
eyes.where: aboard the María Pita and Magallanes; Caribbean, New Spain, Philippines, Macao, Canton, St Helena
eyes.authenticity: His correspondence with the minister José Antonio Caballero, the viceroys and colonial governors, his rolls of the children and staff, and his reports survive in Spanish archives (Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico) and are summarised and partly published in Spanish scholarship; no single diary survives. Dates here follow the published itineraries.
eyes.bio: Balmis had served as a surgeon in Spanish America and translated a French treatise on vaccination. He designed the expedition around children as living carriers, fought officials who thought they had the vaccine already, and pressed for permanent vaccination boards (juntas) to keep it alive after he left. He was often quarrelsome, and his letters show it.

sources.title: AEPap/aeped: La Real Expedición Filantrópica de la Vacuna (itinerary and documents)
PAHO Perspectives in Health: the Balmis expedition
ECU Laupus Library: Chronology of the Balmis Expedition

eyes.name: Isabel Zendal Gómez (Sendales, Cendala)
eyes.role: Rectoress of the Casa de Expósitos (foundling house), A Coruña; the only woman on the expedition; carer of the carrier children
eyes.where: aboard the María Pita and Magallanes; later Puebla, New Spain
eyes.form: named in others' records (no surviving firsthand account found)
eyes.authenticity: No surviving firsthand account found. She is known from Balmis's rolls (30 November 1803; 15 April 1805), his letters from Canton and a letter from Seville of 6 December 1809, which spell her name variously. Her later life in Puebla is probable rather than proven.
eyes.bio: Zendal brought her own adopted son, Benito Vélez, into the expedition as one of the carriers and looked after the boys through two ocean crossings. Balmis praised her in letters from Canton, noting she fell ill herself. What she thought of the voyage is not recorded in her own words.

sources.title: AEPap/aeped: expedition rolls and letters
Balmis Expedition (overview)

eyes.name: José Salvany y Lleopart
eyes.role: Deputy director of the expedition; leader of the South American branch; aged 27 at sailing
eyes.where: New Granada, Quito, Peru, Upper Peru
eyes.form: official letters and reports (with a later recollection of the shipwreck)
eyes.authenticity: Salvany's reports and petitions to the crown and colonial authorities survive in Spanish and South American archives and are cited in Colombian and Spanish scholarship. His timing of the shipwreck comes from a later recollection, not a same-day log.
eyes.bio: Salvany took the harder road: overland and upriver through the Andes for six years, carrying the vaccine in successive groups of local children. He lost the sight of one eye and the use of a wrist, was repeatedly ill, possibly with tuberculosis, and died in Cochabamba without returning to Spain.

sources.title: Academia Nacional de Medicina (Colombia): La Expedición Filantrópica de la Vacuna
El Tiempo: 'la desagradable noticia de haber encallado'
PAHO Perspectives in Health

eyes.name: Francisco Oller y Ferrer
eyes.role: Catalan-born chief surgeon of the military hospital, San Juan, Puerto Rico
eyes.vantage_label: the local vaccinator who came first
eyes.form: official correspondence (known chiefly through the governor's reports)
eyes.authenticity: His work is documented in Puerto Rican and Spanish official papers, including Governor Ramón de Castro's report to the king defending him; no personal diary is known. Dates follow Puerto Rican medical-historical scholarship.
eyes.bio: Oller obtained lymph from vaccinated people on Danish St Thomas and had vaccinated thousands in San Juan before the María Pita arrived. Balmis declared his work ineffective and revaccinated; Oller's supporters noted that his patients did not react to the revaccination, which suggested they were already protected.

sources.title: Galenus: El Dr. Francisco Oller
PAHO Perspectives in Health

eyes.name: Tomás Romay y Chacón
eyes.role: Havana physician and member of the Real Sociedad Económica; Cuba's leading advocate of vaccination
eyes.vantage_label: the creole physician who had already begun
eyes.form: published memoir on vaccination and official reports
eyes.authenticity: Romay's account of introducing the vaccine in Cuba was printed in Havana in the 1800s and is reprinted in his collected works; dates of his first vaccinations are given here only at month precision.
eyes.bio: Romay had vaccine circulating in Havana before Balmis's ship arrived in May 1804, and worked with him to found a Junta Central de Vacuna joined to the Sociedad Económica. His position shows the colonial medical class as partners and rivals rather than passive recipients.

sources.title: AEPap/aeped: Havana stage (26 May–18 June 1804)

eyes.name: José de Iturrigaray y Aróstegui
eyes.vantage_label: the viceroy who disputed the numbers
eyes.authenticity: His exchanges with Balmis (August–September 1804) survive in the Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico, and Spanish archives and are summarised in Spanish scholarship.
eyes.bio: Iturrigaray's government had already obtained vaccine before Balmis arrived and saw less need for him. The quarrel over how many people were still unvaccinated, and over where the Spanish boys should be housed, shows how a royal humanitarian project met a colonial bureaucracy with its own claims.

sources.title: AEPap/aeped: Mexico stage

eyes.name: Alexander Pearson
eyes.role: Surgeon to the British East India Company's factory at Canton and Macao
eyes.authenticity: His 1805 treatise survives in George Thomas Staunton's Chinese translation (Yingjili guo xinchu zhongdou qishu, 1805); his report to the National Vaccine Establishment dated Canton, 18 February 1816, was printed in English.
eyes.bio: Pearson took up the vaccine that reached Macao from Manila in May 1805 and taught Chinese assistants to use it. His 1816 report insisted that Portuguese practitioners had vaccinated in Macao before Balmis arrived — a direct challenge to the expedition's claim to have brought it to China.

sources.title: T. B. Colvin, 'Arms Around the World' (Revista de Cultura 18, 2006), part 1
T. B. Colvin, part 2 (Macao and Canton)

eyes.name: Qiu Xi (Hequa, A Hequa)
eyes.role: Chinese assistant to the foreign merchants at Macao, then Canton's principal vaccinator
eyes.authenticity: His Yindou lüe (Outline of Vaccination) was printed in Canton in 1817 and often reprinted; its account of his own vaccination in 1805 is a later recollection. Dates here are at year or month precision.
eyes.bio: Qiu Xi was vaccinated in Macao in 1805, practised for decades in Canton, and recast the technique in the language of Chinese medicine — channels and points — so that Chinese families would accept it. He is one of the few non-European practitioners in this story who wrote his own account.

sources.title: T. B. Colvin, part 2 (Qiu Xi and the Canton vaccine house)

eyes.name: Robert Squirrell
eyes.role: London medical practitioner and pamphleteer against vaccination
eyes.vantage_label: the rival who said it would not work
eyes.authenticity: Observations addressed to the public in general on the cow-pox (London: W. Smith & Son, 1805) survives in the Wellcome Collection, digitised under the Public Domain Mark.
eyes.bio: Squirrell spoke for the minority of practitioners who held that cowpox was a disease of its own, derived from scrofula, and gave no protection; others in the same year argued that the older smallpox inoculation was safer. His pamphlet shows the expedition sailed while the method was still contested in Jenner's own country.

sources.title: Wellcome Collection: Squirrell, Observations ... on the cow-pox (1805)

entries.headline: Cowpox from a milkmaid's hand into a boy's arm
entries.digest: Jenner took matter from a fresh cowpox sore on the hand of the dairymaid Sarah Nelmes and inserted it through two shallow cuts into the arm of James Phipps, aged eight. The boy had a mild fever and some discomfort around the ninth day and was soon well. In the Inquiry Nelmes is Case XVI and Phipps Case XVII.
entries.source_note: Jenner, Inquiry (1798), Cases XVI–XVII, as summarised by the James Lind Library https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/?p=1128

entries.headline: The deliberate smallpox challenge
entries.digest: About six weeks after the cowpox, Jenner inoculated Phipps with matter from a smallpox sore. No pustule formed and the usual illness did not follow. Jenner treated the boy's body as the test of his whole theory, and reported the result with delight to his friend Edward Gardner in a letter later printed by his biographer.
entries.source_note: Inquiry Case XVII (six weeks); day of the challenge and of the Gardner letter (usually given as 1 and 19 July 1796) not checked here.

entries.headline: The Inquiry goes to press
entries.digest: Jenner published An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae at his own expense: about seventy pages of case histories with coloured plates of Sarah Nelmes's hand and children's arms. Its claim was that cowpox protected people from smallpox. Within two years it had been read, translated and abridged across Europe and the Americas.
entries.source_note: James Lind Library; King's College London exhibition page.

entries.headline: A chain of children, arm to arm
entries.digest: Having waited two years for cowpox to reappear in the local dairies, Jenner vaccinated two five-year-old boys, John Baker and William Summers, on the same day, then carried the matter onward from child to child through four generations, including William Pead. This short chain at home was the method the Spanish expedition would later stretch across oceans.
entries.source_note: Inquiry Cases XVIII–XXIII, James Lind Library summary https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/?p=1128

entries.headline: A Harvard professor vaccinates his own son
entries.digest: Using cowpox matter sent from England, Waterhouse vaccinated his young son Daniel, then other children of his household. It is the first recorded vaccination in the United States. He watched for the pustule and fever exactly as Jenner's plates described.

entries.headline: Seeking the Vice-President's backing
entries.digest: Waterhouse wrote to Thomas Jefferson enclosing his pamphlet A Prospect of Exterminating the Small-Pox. He wanted the authority of a national figure behind a method many American doctors still distrusted.

entries.headline: Thanks for the pamphlet, read last night
entries.digest: Jefferson told Waterhouse he had read the kine-pox pamphlet with great satisfaction, called the discovery a gift to humanity that removed a source of suffering, and said Waterhouse deserved well of his country. It was the start of a correspondence that turned Jefferson into a vaccinator.

entries.headline: Predicting the end of smallpox
entries.digest: In a short pamphlet tracing the history of his discovery, Jenner wrote that so many vaccinations had now been done that the destruction of smallpox must follow from the practice. It was a claim about a disease that was still killing hundreds of thousands a year in Europe alone.
entries.quote: the most dreadful scourge of the human species
entries.source_note: Jenner, The Origin of the Vaccine Inoculation (London, 1801); phrase widely quoted; month of publication not checked.

entries.headline: Live matter by post to Virginia
entries.digest: Waterhouse posted cowpox matter to Jefferson, followed by further packets on 24 and 26 July and 1 August, and promised weekly supplies until one took. Heat and the slow mail killed much of it; the first lot, passed to Dr Edward Gantt in Washington, failed.
entries.source_note: Founders Online, TJ to Waterhouse 8 Aug 1801 and editorial notes https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Jefferson/01-35-02-0037

entries.headline: Six of the household are inoculated
entries.digest: Jefferson reported that Waterhouse's packets of 24 and 26 July had reached Monticello on 6 August, and that a neighbourhood physician, Dr Wardlaw, had inserted the matter into six of 'my own family'. He explained that Virginia law made the old smallpox inoculation rare, so the disease was greatly feared, and hoped to establish vaccination in the district.

entries.headline: Counting the arms that took
entries.digest: Jefferson tallied his trial like a ledger: two, two and four successful takes from the successive packets; fifteen more people vaccinated on 16 August from those arms, fourteen of whom took. Twenty members of his household now showed the disease. Most had only a sore arm; a few had fever, headache or swollen glands. Those vaccinated included enslaved people at Monticello, chosen by him.
entries.source_note: Founders Online https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Jefferson/01-35-02-0093; enslaved people among those vaccinated per Monticello and IU exhibit.

entries.headline: One arm out of twenty takes
entries.digest: Lymph that had come overland from Europe by way of Baghdad was tried on about twenty Bombay children. Only the arm of Anna Dusthall, aged three, produced a proper pustule. Matter from it was used on five more children and packed into vials, and children and vials were sent on to other stations. Nothing survives in her own words or her family's.
entries.source_note: ThePrint excerpt of Yadav https://theprint.in/pageturner/excerpt/indias-first-vaccine-producers-werent-labs-they-were-children-cows-buffaloes-goats/1118187 (age, twenty children, five onward); Homegrown (June 1802, onward routes to Poona, Madras, Calcutta). Day not checked against the original Bombay report.

entries.headline: The Royal Order goes out
entries.digest: A royal order in the name of Charles IV, sent by the minister José Antonio Caballero, announced the expedition to the viceroys of New Spain, Peru, New Granada and Río de la Plata, the captains-general of the Canaries, Caracas and the Philippines, and the governors of Havana and Puerto Rico. Each was told to supply transport, money and boys to carry the vaccine onward.

entries.headline: Lymph from St Thomas takes
entries.digest: Having heard that people on the Danish island of St Thomas had been vaccinated, Oller obtained matter from them on threads and glass, and from a vaccinated girl who came to San Juan. His first successful vaccinations date from 28 November 1803 — two days before the María Pita left Spain.

entries.headline: The María Pita sails with twenty-two boys
entries.digest: The corvette left A Coruña carrying Balmis, his deputy Salvany, assistants, nurses, the rectoress Isabel Zendal and the boys on the roll dated that day: foundlings aged three to nine from the orphanages of A Coruña and Santiago, with Zendal's adopted son Benito Vélez last on the list. Two boys at a time were to be vaccinated from the pustules of the previous two, about every ten days, to keep the cowpox alive.
entries.source_note: aeped (roll of 30 Nov 1803; contract of the María Pita 8 Oct 1803) https://www.aeped.es/sites/default/files/documentos/5.pdf; some sources count 21 or 20 boys.

entries.headline: On the roll: the rectoress and her son
entries.digest: The expedition roll lists the rectoress of the A Coruña foundling house as the only woman aboard, with her adopted son Benito Vélez among the carriers. Her task was to feed, wash and calm the boys through the crossing and keep them apart so the cowpox could be passed in order. No surviving firsthand account found.

entries.headline: Vaccinating the whole town
entries.digest: Systematic vaccination of San Juan began, and by about a month later some 5,000 residents had been vaccinated. When Balmis arrived in February and revaccinated many of them, Oller's supporters reported that they did not react — evidence, they said, that his vaccine had worked. The governor defended him to the king.

entries.headline: Havana starts without the expedition
entries.digest: Vaccine reached Havana from Puerto Rico months before the María Pita, and Romay began vaccinating. When Balmis came he found the practice under way.
entries.source_note: aeped (Romay had introduced the vaccine before the expedition) https://www.aeped.es/sites/default/files/documentos/5.pdf; month from Romay's published account, not checked here.

entries.headline: Arriving to find the vaccine already there
entries.digest: After five weeks among the Canary Islands and the Atlantic crossing, the expedition reached San Juan and found that the surgeon Francisco Oller had been vaccinating since November with lymph from St Thomas. Balmis declared Oller's vaccinations unreliable and had people revaccinated, including the bishop. Governor Ramón de Castro sided with Oller.

entries.headline: A vaccine board for Caracas
entries.digest: Landing at Puerto Cabello on 20 March after a hard passage, Balmis vaccinated 28 local children there to renew the chain, then reached Caracas on 28 March. A mass vaccination followed in Holy Week, and the Junta Central de Vacuna set up in Caracas became his model for keeping the vaccine alive after the expedition moved on. The young Andrés Bello wrote an ode to the vaccine that April.

entries.headline: The expedition splits in two
entries.digest: Following written instructions Balmis had issued on 29 April, Salvany sailed from La Guaira on the brig San Luis with three assistants and four boys for New Granada and Peru. Balmis kept the María Pita for Havana and New Spain, with Isabel Zendal and six boys among his party.

entries.place: Bocas de Ceniza, mouth of the Magdalena
entries.headline: Wrecked at the mouth of the Magdalena
entries.digest: Six days out of La Guaira the San Luis ran aground at one of the Magdalena's mouths. Salvany later recalled the moment as four minutes past midnight on the 13th, which was strictly already the 14th. The party and the four boys were taken off to a deserted beach by a coastguard vessel; no one died, but instruments were lost and the ship broke up.
entries.source_note: El Tiempo https://www.eltiempo.com/salud/la-desagradable-noticia-de-haber-encallado-3437711 (Salvany's later recollection); aeped (13 May) https://www.aeped.es/sites/default/files/documentos/5.pdf

entries.headline: On foot into Cartagena
entries.digest: Salvany's party reached Cartagena overland and began vaccinating. After a month he left again on 24 June with ten local children taken from Cartagena to carry the vaccine up the Magdalena towards Santafé.

entries.headline: Receiving the royal expedition
entries.digest: Balmis arrived on 26 May and stayed until 18 June. Rather than fight, Romay helped found a Junta Central de Vacuna merged with the Sociedad Económica, which carried on vaccinating in Cuba after the expedition left.

entries.headline: News of the wreck reaches Havana
entries.digest: In Havana, Balmis learned from the Cartagena mail that the San Luis had run aground at one of the mouths of the Magdalena. He reported the 'unpleasant news' to Spain. To carry the vaccine on to Yucatán he needed new carriers; accounts of the Havana stage record enslaved children among them.
entries.source_note: aeped (date news received) https://www.aeped.es/sites/default/files/documentos/5.pdf; El Tiempo (Balmis's report) https://www.eltiempo.com/salud/la-desagradable-noticia-de-haber-encallado-3437711; enslaved carriers per Balmis Expedition overview https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balmis_Expedition

entries.headline: Landfall in New Spain
entries.digest: After landing at Sisal in Yucatán on 25 June and a ten-day crossing, the expedition reached Veracruz. Balmis pressed on towards Mexico City, where the Spanish boys were to be housed, schooled and, in the end, left behind.

entries.headline: A quarrel with the viceroy over numbers
entries.digest: Balmis wrote to Viceroy Iturrigaray about how many people in New Spain were still unvaccinated, arguing for his own programme. The viceroy answered the next day disputing his figures. On 6 September Balmis submitted a plan for keeping the vaccine alive in the capital.

entries.headline: The viceroy disputes the figures
entries.digest: The day after Balmis's letter, Iturrigaray replied disputing his estimate of the unvaccinated population: vaccine had already been circulating in New Spain before the expedition arrived. The quarrel extended to the boys' care — they were lodged in the Real Hospicio, a setting Balmis objected to.

entries.headline: Leaving the Spanish boys in the viceroy's care
entries.digest: Before the Pacific leg, the boys from A Coruña were placed in the viceroy's charge. An inspector later reported that six of the fourteen boys over six attended school; others were placed in the Escuela Patriótica founded in 1806, and the rest were adopted by Mexican families.

entries.headline: Bogotá, two years after an epidemic
entries.digest: Arriving in the viceregal capital, where a smallpox epidemic had struck two years before, Salvany stayed about three months and met the botanist José Celestino Mutis. The expedition counted more than 56,000 vaccinations from Cartagena to the capital. On the journey he lost the sight of one eye and the use of a wrist.
entries.source_note: aeped https://www.aeped.es/sites/default/files/documentos/5.pdf; PAHO (18 Dec) https://www3.paho.org/English/DD/PIN/Number11_article6.htm; Academia Nacional de Medicina https://encolombia.com/medicina/revistas-medicas/academedicina/vam-129/expedicion-filantropica-vacuna/

entries.headline: A London practitioner says cowpox protects no one
entries.digest: In a pamphlet addressed to the public, Squirrell argued that cowpox originated in scrofula and gave no security against smallpox, and he made observations in favour of the old inoculation with smallpox itself. The same year George Lipscomb published a defence of inoculation as safer than vaccination.

entries.headline: Twenty-six Mexican boys for the Pacific
entries.digest: Balmis embarked on the galleon Magallanes for Manila with Zendal and 26 Mexican boys gathered as new carriers for the ten-week crossing. The Spanish boys from A Coruña stayed behind in New Spain. Two of the original boys, Tomás Melitón and Juan Antonio, are recorded as having died.
entries.source_note: aeped (8 Feb; 26 boys; deaths) https://www.aeped.es/sites/default/files/documentos/5.pdf; ECU chronology gives 9 Feb https://hsl.ecu.edu/wp-content/pv-uploads/sites/216/2017/09/Chronology-Smallpox-and-Balmis-Expedition.pdf

entries.headline: The galleon reaches Manila Bay
entries.digest: The Magallanes arrived on 15 April and vaccination began next day. By early August about 9,000 people had been vaccinated in and around the capital. The governor-general vaccinated his own children to win over a reluctant clergy. Balmis's list of personnel dated this day names 'doña Isabel Zendala y Gómez'.

entries.headline: Vaccine arrives from Manila on a Portuguese ship
entries.digest: The Portuguese merchant Pedro Huet brought his ship Esperanza back from Manila to Macao with his crew vaccinated, carrying the vaccine in their arms. Portuguese practitioners began vaccinating at the Santa Casa da Misericórdia, and Pearson took it up for both foreigners and Chinese in Macao and Canton.

entries.headline: Vaccinated himself, then his family
entries.digest: Qiu Xi, working for the foreign merchants at Macao, had himself vaccinated when the vaccine arrived in 1805, then had it given to his family. He later wrote that seeing it work persuaded him to learn the method.
entries.source_note: Colvin part 2 https://www.icm.gov.mo/rc/viewer/pdfViewerParts/40018/3767; Qiu Xi, Yindou lüe (1817) preface, a later recollection.

entries.headline: Over the Andes to Quito
entries.digest: After Popayán, where his illness returned, Salvany reached Quito and stayed two months before going south through Cuenca and Loja, where thousands more were vaccinated. Each stage needed a new group of local children to keep the cowpox alive.
entries.source_note: Academia Nacional de Medicina https://encolombia.com/medicina/revistas-medicas/academedicina/vam-129/expedicion-filantropica-vacuna/; aeped; PAHO (Cuenca 7,000; Loja 3,500)

entries.headline: A treatise translated into Chinese
entries.digest: Pearson's short treatise on vaccination appeared in a Chinese translation by George Thomas Staunton, the East India Company's young interpreter, as Yingjili guo xinchu zhongdou qishu ('A curious book on the newly arrived English method of planting smallpox'), printed with the support of James Drummond and the hong merchant Gnewqua.

entries.headline: Three Filipino boys and a typhoon
entries.digest: Balmis left Manila for Macao on the Portuguese frigate called the Diligencia with his assistant Francisco Pastor and three boys supplied by the curate of Santa Cruz, leaving the Mexican boys to be taken home. A typhoon struck near Macao and the party landed after several days of storm.

entries.headline: Praised by Balmis, ill herself
entries.digest: In letters written from Canton, Balmis praised Zendal's devotion to the children on the Pacific crossing and noted that she had fallen ill herself during the voyage. She seems to have remained in New Spain afterwards, probably in Puebla, with Benito. Her own words do not survive.
entries.source_note: aeped (Balmis letters from Canton) https://www.aeped.es/sites/default/files/documentos/5.pdf; Puebla residence 'possible' in that study.

entries.headline: Forty days in Canton, about twenty vaccinated
entries.digest: Balmis went up to Canton hoping to plant the vaccine in China and sought help from the East India Company. In about forty days he vaccinated only some twenty people. He found the Company's surgeon and Portuguese practitioners in Macao already vaccinating with lymph that had come from Manila in May.

entries.headline: The chain breaks in Canton
entries.digest: Qiu Xi began vaccinating in Canton and became its principal practitioner. That same year the lymph died out locally, and foreign surgeons had to obtain fresh vaccine again — a recurring problem until children were regularly brought from Luzon to restart it, as in 1810.

entries.headline: Ten years to the day after Phipps
entries.digest: Writing to Jenner on the tenth anniversary of the first vaccination, Jefferson thanked him, said he had been an early convert and recommended it to his countrymen, and ranked it above Harvey's discovery of the circulation of the blood. He predicted that future nations would know of smallpox only from history.
entries.quote: the loathsome small-pox has existed and by you has been extirpated

entries.headline: Lima says it has no need of him
entries.digest: In Lima the city council told Salvany that the vaccine had already arrived — it had come overland from Buenos Aires, having reached the Río de la Plata in the arms of enslaved people shipped from Brazil to Montevideo. Only after the new viceroy Abascal arrived in August did the authorities back him; the expedition then counted 22,726 vaccinated in the kingdom of Peru.

entries.headline: Vaccinating an enemy island
entries.digest: On the voyage home on the Portuguese ship Bom Jesus de Além, Balmis put in at the British island of St Helena, though Spain and Britain were at war, and vaccinated there under Governor Robert Patton. On 16 June he was handed a sealed packet with lymph and handwritten instructions from Jenner.

entries.headline: Reporting to the king
entries.digest: Having landed at Lisbon on 14 August, Balmis was received by Charles IV at San Ildefonso and reported that he had carried the vaccine around the world. On 4 December he sent the minister Caballero a written summary of the expedition's costs and results.
entries.source_note: aeped (7 Sept; 4 Dec letter) https://www.aeped.es/sites/default/files/documentos/5.pdf; ECU gives 17 Sept https://hsl.ecu.edu/wp-content/pv-uploads/sites/216/2017/09/Chronology-Smallpox-and-Balmis-Expedition.pdf

entries.headline: Jenner hears of the Spanish voyage
entries.digest: Writing to the Rev. Mr Dibbin, Jenner reported the news that the Spanish expedition had carried the vaccine around the globe. He judged it unmatched in history as an act of philanthropy. He had himself sent lymph and written instructions that reached Balmis at St Helena in June.
entries.quote: an example of philanthropy so noble, so extensive as this
entries.source_note: Letter to Dibbin, 22 Nov 1806, quoted in PAHO Perspectives in Health https://www3.paho.org/English/DD/PIN/Number11_article6.htm; printed in Baron, Life of Jenner.

entries.headline: Death in Cochabamba
entries.digest: Salvany died in Cochabamba aged about 34, still waiting for the financial support he had asked of the Audiencia. He had spent six years on the road and never returned to Spain. Balmis informed the Cortes of his death in March 1813.
entries.source_note: aeped https://www.aeped.es/sites/default/files/documentos/5.pdf; PAHO; Academia Nacional de Medicina

entries.headline: Who brought the vaccine to China
entries.digest: In a report to the National Vaccine Establishment in London, Pearson stated that Portuguese practitioners had vaccinated in Macao before Balmis arrived, and estimated that thousands had been vaccinated in a twelve-month period. He described Chinese vaccinators trained by him carrying on the practice in Canton.

entries.headline: Writing vaccination into Chinese medicine
entries.digest: Qiu Xi published his Yindou lüe, describing vaccination in the terms of Chinese medicine and recounting his own experience since 1805. The book was reprinted many times and carried the method beyond Canton.
entries.source_note: Colvin part 2 https://www.icm.gov.mo/rc/viewer/pdfViewerParts/40018/3767 (Qiu Xi's role); date of first printing as usually given.

convergences.label: 14 May 1796 and 14 May 1806: the first vaccination and its tenth anniversary
convergences.note: Jenner's case note on Phipps and Jefferson's letter to Jenner fall on the same date ten years apart: the experiment on one child at Berkeley and a President's prediction that smallpox would become a thing of history.

convergences.label: Summer 1800 to summer 1802: the vaccine reaches America and India by other roads
convergences.note: Matter posted on threads from England to Cambridge, Massachusetts, and on to Monticello, and lymph sent overland via Baghdad to Bombay: dried vaccine sometimes survived, but each time most of it failed and everything depended on one or two arms that took.

convergences.label: Balmis lands at San Juan
convergences.note: The royal expedition and the local surgeon each claimed the genuine vaccine. Balmis revaccinated; Oller's side read the absence of a reaction as proof of earlier protection. The governor sided with Oller.

convergences.label: May 1804: the split, the wreck and Havana
convergences.note: Within three weeks Salvany's brig was wrecked at the Magdalena, Balmis reached a Havana where Romay was already vaccinating, and the news of the wreck caught up with him there.

convergences.label: Mexico City, late August 1804
convergences.note: The director and the viceroy argued over numbers and over the boys' lodging while Zendal kept charge of the children who had carried the vaccine across the Atlantic — the one party whose view is not recorded.

convergences.label: Macao and Canton, May–October 1805
convergences.note: Vaccine reached Macao from Manila in the arms of a Portuguese crew months before Balmis; when he arrived he found Pearson and his Chinese pupil Qiu Xi already at work, and Pearson's 1816 report later disputed the expedition's priority.

convergences.label: St Helena, June 1806
convergences.note: On a British island in wartime, the Spanish director vaccinated the population and received a packet of lymph and instructions from Jenner — the two ends of the story meeting by post.

convergences.label: Late 1806: verdicts
convergences.note: Jenner praised the voyage as unmatched philanthropy and Balmis summarised its costs for the minister, while Salvany, in Peru, was only halfway through a journey that would end with his death.

ties.note: Waterhouse built his practice on Jenner's Inquiry and obtained his first matter from England.
They corresponded from December 1800; Waterhouse supplied the matter Jefferson used at Monticello in 1801.
Jefferson wrote to Jenner on 14 May 1806 praising the discovery.
Jenner's lymph and written instructions reached Balmis at St Helena; Jenner praised the expedition in November 1806.
Director and deputy; Balmis issued Salvany's instructions on 29 April 1804 before the expedition split at La Guaira.
Zendal served under Balmis through both ocean crossings; he named and praised her in his rolls and letters.
Balmis declared Oller's vaccinations ineffective; the governor of Puerto Rico defended Oller to the king.
In Havana they founded a vaccine board together, though Romay had begun first.
Their August 1804 letters disputed the numbers still unvaccinated and the care of the boys.
Both worked in Macao and Canton in autumn 1805; Pearson's 1816 report rejected the claim that Balmis first brought the vaccine to China.
Qiu Xi learned vaccination among the foreign practitioners at Macao and became the leading vaccinator of Canton.
Squirrell's 1805 pamphlet denied that Jenner's cowpox protected anyone.

threads_out.note: Smallpox reached Mexico with the Spanish in 1520 and devastated Tenochtitlan; 284 years later a Spanish royal expedition brought the vaccine against it to the same land.
Boston's 1721 inoculation controversy introduced smallpox inoculation to New England; in 1800 another Boston-area physician, Benjamin Waterhouse, introduced vaccination there.
Japan's Dutch-learning (rangaku) physicians, heirs of the 1771 Edo dissection, obtained viable vaccine only in 1849, through the Dutch post at Dejima in Nagasaki.
Pearson and Qiu Xi worked within the Canton trading system of the East India Company and the hong merchants, the same system whose collapse led to the Opium War.
Bombay, where vaccination in British India began with Anna Dusthall's arm in 1802, was the city where plague broke out in 1896 and where Waldemar Haffkine developed and tested his plague vaccine.
